title: Judgment (CCC 1021–1022)
hook: at death each person is judged by love

segments.voice: Yesterday, memento mori: remembering death to live well. Your line was remember you will die. Did you write down your sentence? Today, what Catholics say happens the moment after. Day three hundred twenty-five.

A courtroom. A huge book. Every lie you ever told, read out loud. A stern face, a gavel. Maybe a scale, with your good deeds on one side and your bad ones on the other, and you watching to see which way it tips. That's the picture the word judgment can drag in behind it. Now hold it next to a sentence from a Spanish friar you met earlier on this path, John of the Cross: at the evening of life, he said, we will be judged on love. Not on the scale. On love. Today, what the Church means.
screen: `A COURTROOM, A BOOK, A GAVEL.` → `A SCALE THAT TIPS.` → `JUDGED ON LOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The letter to the Hebrews says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment." The Catechism teaches that each person receives this judgment at the very moment of death. It's called the particular judgment, because it's about one particular life. Second, it's immediate. The Catechism says that at death each soul receives its eternal destiny at once: heaven, either through a purification or directly, or else separation from God forever. Catholics point to the thief crucified next to Jesus, who asked only to be remembered, and heard: "this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Not someday. Today. Third, on love. The Catechism quotes John of the Cross's line about being judged on love at the evening of life. It fits Jesus's own story of the sheep and the goats, where the question isn't how much you knew but whether you fed the hungry. Catholics say that at death a person sees their life in Christ's light, and the question is how they loved, and whether they accepted or refused his love. Fourth, two judgments. The Church also speaks of a final judgment at the end of time, when Christ returns and everything, the whole of history, is brought into the light. The particular judgment is one life. The last judgment is all of them together. And the one who judges, Catholics say, is the same one who died for the person being judged. Justice, yes, they say, but from a judge who wants each person home.
screen: `ONCE TO DIE, AND AFTER, JUDGMENT.` · `THIS DAY, IN PARADISE.` · `JUDGED ON LOVE.` · `ONE LIFE, THEN ALL OF THEM.` · then, large: `JUDGED BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: examine one relationship. Settle, and breathe. Choose one person close to you: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, a coworker. Look at the last month with them honestly, in a kind light. Where did you love well? Name it. Where did love run thin, a short word, a missed call, a silence? Name that too, without beating yourself up. Then ask one question: what would more love look like here, this week? If you pray, you can ask for help to do it. The bell holds the time.
Judgment. In Catholic teaching, the moment at death when each life is seen in Christ's light, and judged on love, followed by a final judgment at the end of time. Today's word.
Your line: judged by love. Today, do the one thing more love would look like with the person you chose. Day three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, and many make a nightly examination of conscience, looking back over the day with the question of how they loved.

notes: Douay-Rheims Hebrews 9:27 and Luke 23:43 given from memory; confirm wording.
John of the Cross's saying is paraphrased (modern translations are under copyright); reference Sayings of Light and Love 64, quoted in CCC 1022. Confirm.

CCC 1022 wording 'enters either a purification, or heaven directly, or chooses to be separated from God' is a paraphrase of 'either entrance into the blessedness of heaven—through a purification or immediately,—or immediate and everlasting damnation'. Keeper should confirm the softer phrasing is faithful.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener 'most of us picture'; cut the unsourced 'sixteenth-century'; the CCC 1022 paraphrase was garbled ('enters ... or chooses') and softened damnation into a choice, so it now follows CCC 1022 (heaven through a purification or immediately, or separation from God forever); 'someone who wants you home' reframed as what Catholics say.
